approachQuestion.prompt:
Telemetry arrival checks

An immutable array contains n half-open listening windows [start,end), sorted by start and pairwise non-overlapping: end[i] ≤ start[i+1]. A stream supplies q arrival times one at a time. For each arrival t, return whether start ≤ t < end for any window, before the next arrival is supplied. The arrays support constant-time indexed reads. No preprocessing, copying or persistent index is allowed; each query must be answered from the supplied windows using only a fixed number of temporary variables.

Input: windows = [[2,5],[5,8],[11,14]], arrivals = [1,5,8,13,14]
Output, in arrival order: [false,true,false,true,false]

Input: windows = [[0,1],[9,10]], arrivals = [0,7]
Output: [true,false]

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ q ≤ 200000; integer endpoints satisfy 0 ≤ start < end ≤ 1000000000; 0 ≤ t ≤ 1000000000. Arrival times have no ordering guarantee. Only comparisons of times and constant-time index arithmetic are available; do not use coordinate-indexed lookup. Choose the best worst-case total running time subject to the memory and online-answer requirements.

options.text: For each t, binary-search for the last window whose start is at most t. Return true exactly when such a window exists and t is strictly less than its end.
options.feedback: The predecessor is the only possible containing window: every later window starts too late, and every earlier window ends no later than this candidate starts. The final end comparison detects gaps.

options.text: For each t, binary-search for the first window whose end is strictly greater than t. Return true exactly when such a window exists and its start is at most t.
options.feedback: Non-overlap also makes ends strictly increasing. The first end beyond t is the only possible candidate; checking its start rejects a gap. This has the same cost and endpoint behavior as searching starts.

options.text: For every arrival, scan windows from the beginning until a containing window is found or the next start exceeds t.
options.feedback: This is correct and uses the permitted memory, but an arrival after every window forces a full scan each time. It ignores the ability to discard half of the ordered candidates at each comparison.

options.text: Binary-search for the last start at most t, then return true when t is at most that window’s end.
options.feedback: The end of a half-open window is excluded. For windows [[2,5],[9,12]] and arrival 5, this returns true although no window contains 5.

feedback.reason: Reduce point membership in separated intervals to one boundary search and a final containment test.
details: For each arriving time independently, use an iterative binary search over the window starts to find the last start at most that time. If none exists return false; otherwise compare the time with that candidate’s end using a strict less-than test. Keep only search bounds, a candidate index and the current time. Answer before reading the next arrival.

The last start no greater than the arrival is the only candidate in sorted disjoint windows. Its end test remains strict for half-open membership. Independent arrivals need not be chronological, so do not retain a forward-only query cursor.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For predecessor-start-search, what is the tightest standard worst-case total time for all q online arrivals and auxiliary space? n ≥ 2. Search directly in the supplied array; there is no preprocessing and no copy. Answers may be emitted immediately, and any collected answer list is returned output.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

options.text: Time O(q log n), auxiliary space O(n)
Time O(q log n), auxiliary space O(1)

feedback.reason: Each arrival performs its own logarithmic start-boundary search.
details: Each independent binary search halves the remaining candidate range and takes logarithmic worst-case time, followed by one end check. Over q arrivals the costs add. Fixed search variables use constant auxiliary memory; there is no copy, index structure, recursion or hashing. The forward scan alternative is correct but may inspect every window for every arrival.
Comparison-only online queries; n≥2; iterative binary search on immutable random-access input; returned answers excluded.
“Time O(n+q), auxiliary space O(1)”: Independent arrivals are not ordered, so a single forward scan cannot serve the entire stream. Each specified search may require logarithmically many comparisons.
“Time O(q log n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The binary search reads the original array directly and is iterative. There is no index copy or growing search stack.
“Time O(nq), auxiliary space O(1)”: A full scan describes another option. The specified binary search halves its candidate range each step, so linear work per query is not tight.
